---
title: "Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball"
subtitle: "Seven officials, three ways into the replay booth, and the handful of rules that decide who has the ball, so you can call it before the referee turns on his microphone."
description: "The seven-person NFL officiating crew (referee, umpire, down judge, line judge, side judge, field judge, back judge): where each one stands and what each one watches. Replay in three doors: the coach's challenge (two, plus a third if either succeeds, since 2024), booth review (scoring plays, turnovers, tries and the final two minutes of each half) and replay assist (the 2025 power to overturn certain flags, the 2026 consult on ejections), and why there is still no sky judge. The rules of the ball: the 2018 catch rule and the plays that forced it, down by contact, forward progress, fumble versus incomplete pass, the fumble through the end zone, backward versus forward passes, and intentional grounding and the tackle box. How to read a referee's announcement, the 2025 Hawk-Eye virtual measurement, and what nflverse data says about replay and about crews."
glossary:
  "Referee": "The crew chief of the seven NFL officials, the only one in a white cap. He stands 10 to 12 yards behind the line in the offensive backfield, on the side of the quarterback's throwing arm, watches the quarterback and hits on him, rules on the quarterback's fumbles and passes, and announces every foul and replay result over his microphone."
  "Umpire": "The official responsible for the interior line: holding, false starts and illegal hands among the center, guards and the defenders across from them. Since 2010 he usually stands in the offensive backfield, opposite the referee; he also spots the ball after most plays and checks equipment."
  "Down judge": "The official who straddles the line of scrimmage on one sideline (the side with the chain crew). He rules on offside, encroachment, false starts and illegal formations on his side, watches the receivers and the sideline nearest him, marks forward progress and runs the chain crew. Called the head linesman until 2017."
  "Line judge": "The official who straddles the line of scrimmage on the sideline opposite the down judge, with the same duties on his side: offside, false starts, illegal formation, the near receivers and sideline, forward progress, and whether a pass was thrown from beyond the line."
  "Side judge": "The deep official on the down judge's side, about 20 yards past the line near the sideline. He watches the receivers on his side for pass interference, illegal contact and holding, and rules on catches and out of bounds near his sideline."
  "Field judge": "The deep official on the line judge's side, about 20 yards past the line near the sideline, with the same job as the side judge on that half of the field. On field goals he stands under one upright."
  "Back judge": "The deepest official, about 25 yards past the line in the middle of the field. He watches the tight end and inside receivers, the deep middle and the end line, and stands under the other upright on field goals."
  "Coach's challenge": "A head coach's request, made by throwing a red flag before the next snap, for a replay review of a reviewable ruling. Each team gets two per game, plus a third if either of the first two succeeds (since 2024); a team must have a timeout to challenge and loses it if the challenge fails. Not allowed inside the final two minutes of a half or in overtime, where the booth reviews instead."
  "Replay review": "Checking an on-field ruling against video. The ruling is reversed only if the video shows clear and obvious evidence that it was wrong; otherwise it 'stands' (not enough evidence either way) or is 'confirmed' (the video supports it). In the NFL the final decision is made by the league's officiating staff in New York, with the referee."
  "Booth review": "A replay review started by the replay official in the stadium (or the officiating command center in New York), not by a coach. It covers every scoring play, every turnover, every try, and reviewable plays in the final two minutes of each half and in overtime."
  "Replay assist": "The replay booth's quick, no-stoppage help to the on-field crew on clear-cut objective facts (possession, the spot, whether a catch was completed, whether a player was down or out of bounds, the clock). Since 2025 it may also wipe out certain flags (face mask, horse-collar, tripping, hits on a defenseless player, roughing or running into the kicker), but it cannot add a foul nobody called. Since 2026 league officiating staff may also consult on ejections for flagrant acts."
  "Catch (completed pass)": "Under the rule rewritten in 2018, a player catches a forward pass when he (1) secures control of the ball in his hands or arms before it touches the ground, (2) touches the ground in bounds with both feet or another body part other than his hands, and then (3) makes an act common to the game, such as tucking the ball, turning upfield or reaching for the line, or keeps control long enough to do so. The same test decides an interception."
  "Forward progress": "The farthest point toward the opponent's goal that the ball reached before the ball carrier was stopped. The ball is spotted there, not where he ended up after being driven back, and officials blow the play dead once his progress is stopped."
  "Down by contact": "The NFL's rule for ending a run: the ball carrier is down when any part of his body other than his hands or feet touches the ground after he has been touched by an opponent. A runner who slips untouched may get up and keep going (in college he is down when his knee hits)."
  "Fumble through the end zone (touchback)": "A fumble that goes forward into the opponent's end zone and out of bounds there (out the side or the back). The offense loses the ball even though nobody recovered it: it is a touchback, and the defense takes over at its own 20."
  "Backward pass": {def: "Any pass that is not forward, including one thrown straight across the field parallel to the line. Anyone may throw one at any time, from anywhere; if it hits the ground the ball is still live, so either team may recover it, and advance it.", aliases: ["Lateral"]}
  "Intentional grounding": "A foul by a passer who, facing an imminent loss of yardage, throws a pass that isn't in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver. It costs a loss of down and 10 yards (or the spot of the pass, if that is worse), and a safety if he throws it from his own end zone. A passer who is or has been outside the tackle box may throw it away freely if the ball reaches the line of scrimmage."
  "Tackle box": "The area between the outside edges of where the two offensive tackles lined up, from the line of scrimmage back to the offense's own end line; in the rulebook, the 'pocket area'. Inside it, a throwaway must go near an eligible receiver; once the passer, or the ball, has been outside it, a throwaway only has to reach the line of scrimmage."
  "Virtual measurement": {def: "The NFL's camera-based first-down measurement, used since 2025: a Sony Hawk-Eye system of six 8K cameras in every stadium measures from the officials' spot of the ball to the line to gain, in place of the chain crew walking onto the field. The officials still spot the ball by eye, and the chains stay on the sideline as a backup.", aliases: ["Hawk-Eye measurement"]}

#| code-summary: "Show the Python (drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import logging
import os
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Polygon, Rectangle
from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, defense, routes as r, style, draw_marker, draw_frame
from gridiron.field import FIELD_WIDTH, HASH_NEAR, HASH_FAR, MIDDLE

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
GREEN = "#0f7a55"            # darker step of the aqua highlight: "legal" on the light field
RED = style.SERIES[7]        # "foul"
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]     # the tackle box
ZEBRA = style.INK            # officials: white disc, black ring
BOX_W = 2 * 1.6 + 0.8        # outside edge of a tackle's normal position, yards from the ball


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=""):
    """An offensive (blue) player at (d, w): d = yards downfield of the line, w = yards to the offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=""):
    """A defensive (orange) player."""
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def XY(fld, p, d, w):
    """(d, w) in the offense's frame -> plot coordinates on a drawn field."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True, rot=0):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w), on a light pad so lines underneath don't cut it."""
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    kw = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92) if box else None
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.12, bbox=kw, rotation=rot)


def path_arrow(fld, p, pts, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2.5, 2)), head=9, z=7, rad=0.0):
    """A dashed arrow through (d, w) points: a ball's flight or a loose ball's bounce."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    if len(xy) > 2:
        xs, ys = zip(*xy[:-1])
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color,
                                     lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z, connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def xmark(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ms=8):
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot(x, y, marker="x", ms=ms, mew=2.2, color=color, zorder=11)


def ball_at(fld, p, d, w):
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    draw_marker(fld.ax, x, y, "ball", "", fld.pts_per_yard())


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers: on zoomed diagrams they compete with the labels."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit():
            t.remove()


def official(ax, x, y, label, ppy, r=1.1, alpha=1.0):
    """An official: white disc with a black ring (offense = blue disc, defense = orange square)."""
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r, fc="white", ec=ZEBRA, lw=1.6, zorder=9, alpha=alpha))
    fs = max(4.6, min(8.0, ppy * (1.0 if len(label) == 1 else 0.86)))
    ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=ZEBRA, fontweight="bold", zorder=10,
            alpha=alpha)


def marker_legend(ax, y=-0.01, extra=()):
    h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor="white", ms=8,
                label="Offense"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="D", ls="", markerfacecolor=style.DEFENSE_TINT, markeredgecolor=style.DEFENSE,
                ms=7, label="Defense"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=ZEBRA, mew=1.6, ms=9,
                label="Official")] + list(extra)
    ax.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=len(h), fontsize=7.2,
              frameon=False, handletextpad=0.4, columnspacing=1.2)


def tackle_box(ax, fld, p, back, alpha=0.10):
    """The shaded tackle box (the rulebook's pocket area), from the line back to depth `back`."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in [(-0.7, -BOX_W), (-0.7, BOX_W), (back, BOX_W), (back, -BOX_W)]]
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=PURPLE, alpha=alpha, ec=PURPLE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)),
                         zorder=1.4))


# --- flowchart pieces ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def fbox(ax, x, y, w, h, title, body="", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.7, lw=1.0):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=1.1",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=3))
    if body:
        ax.text(x, y + h / 2 - 1.6, title, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=tfs, fontweight="bold",
                color=style.INK, zorder=4, linespacing=1.1)
        nl = title.count("\n") + 1
        ax.text(x, y + h / 2 - 1.9 - 2.9 * nl, body, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=bfs, color=style.INK_2,
                zorder=4, linespacing=1.18)
    else:
        ax.text(x, y, title, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=tfs, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
                zorder=4, linespacing=1.15)


def farrow(ax, p0, p1, text=None, color=style.INK_2, toff=(0.0, 0.0), ha="center", fs=6.8):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(p0, p1, arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=1.0,
                                 shrinkA=1, shrinkB=1, zorder=2))
    if text:
        ax.text((p0[0] + p1[0]) / 2 + toff[0], (p0[1] + p1[1]) / 2 + toff[1], text, ha=ha, va="center",
                fontsize=fs, color=color, fontweight="bold", zorder=5,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))


def canvas(w_in, h_in, xmax=100, ymax=None):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(w_in, h_in))
    ymax = ymax or xmax * h_in / w_in
    ax.set_xlim(0, xmax); ax.set_ylim(0, ymax); ax.set_axis_off(); ax.grid(False)
    return fig, ax


# --- scenes: simulated tracking plus extra actors (officials), as a video or a frame strip ------
def kf_interp(kf, t):
    kf = np.asarray(kf, dtype=float)
    return np.array([np.interp(t, kf[:, 0], kf[:, 1]), np.interp(t, kf[:, 0], kf[:, 2])])


def draw_scene(ax, play, trk, t, window, lateral, extra=None, decor=None, trails=True, clock=True):
    """One moment of a play on `ax`: players (and ball) from tracking `trk`, extra actors from keyframes."""
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[1], play.ball_y - lateral[0]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, to_go=play.to_go, lateral=(ylo, yhi))
    no_numbers(ax)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    if decor:
        decor(fld, t)
    times = trk.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((times - t).abs().idxmin())
    cur = trk[trk.frameId == fid]
    hist = trk[trk.frameId <= fid] if trails else None
    draw_frame(fld, cur, hist, ppy)
    for key, (lab, kf) in (extra or {}).items():
        ts = np.linspace(min(np.asarray(kf)[:, 0].min(), 0), t, 30)
        pts = np.array([kf_interp(kf, s) for s in ts])
        xs, ys = zip(*[XY(fld, play, d, w) for d, w in pts])
        if trails:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=ZEBRA, lw=0.9, alpha=0.35, zorder=3)
        official(ax, xs[-1], ys[-1], lab, ppy, r=1.15)
    for art in list(ax.patches) + list(ax.texts) + list(ax.lines):
        art.set_clip_on(True)                   # players who ran out of the window don't spill outside it
    if clock:
        ax.set_title("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s", fontsize=8.6, color=style.INK_2)
    return fld


def show_scene(play, trk, times, window, lateral, extra=None, decor=None, notes=None, ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    """HTML: a video of the scene. PDF: a frame strip at `times`, each panel with its note."""
    trk = trk.copy()
    trk["_id"] = trk["displayName"].astype(str)
    if PDF:
        n = len(times)
        nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
        span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
        pw = width_in / ncols
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + 0.35)),
                                 squeeze=False)
        for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
            ax.axis("off")
        for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
            fld = draw_scene(ax, play, trk, t, window, lateral, extra, decor)
            if notes:
                notes(fld, i, t)
        fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0, w_pad=0.6)
        plt.show()
        return
    tmax = float(trk["time"].max())
    t0 = float(trk["time"].min())
    ts = np.round(np.arange(max(t0, -0.5), tmax + 1e-9, 0.1), 2)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 5.6 * span_d / span_w))
    hold = {}

    def update(t):
        ax.clear()
        fld = draw_scene(ax, play, trk, float(t), window, lateral, extra, decor)
        if notes:
            # show the note of the last panel time already passed
            k = max([i for i, tt in enumerate(times) if tt <= t + 1e-6] or [0])
            notes(fld, k, float(t))
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=ts, interval=100, blit=False)
    if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
        html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
    else:
        html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def md_table(rows, header, align):
    lines = ["| " + " | ".join(header) + " |", "|" + "|".join(align) + "|"]
    lines += ["| " + " | ".join(map(str, row)) + " |" for row in rows]
    return Markdown("\n".join(lines))

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load officials, penalties and replay reviews from nflverse)"
#| output: false
import re
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))     # 2016-2025, the last ten completed seasons
cols = ["game_id", "old_game_id", "season", "season_type", "penalty", "desc", "replay_or_challenge"]
raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
raw["desc"] = raw["desc"].fillna("")
S = {}                                # numbers quoted in the text

# --- accepted penalties per game, by the referee who led the crew -------------------------------
# nflverse play text writes an accepted foul as "PENALTY on ..." and a declined or offsetting one as
# "Penalty on ...", so counting the capitalised form counts accepted fouls (both teams, every play).
raw["accepted"] = raw["desc"].str.count("PENALTY on")
games = raw.groupby(["old_game_id", "season", "season_type"], as_index=False)["accepted"].sum()
offs = nfl().load_officials().to_pandas()
refs = (offs[offs.position == "Referee"][["game_id", "season", "official_name"]]
        .rename(columns={"game_id": "old_game_id", "official_name": "referee"}))
games = games.merge(refs, on=["old_game_id", "season"], how="left")
reg = games[games.season_type == "REG"]
by_season = reg.groupby("season")["accepted"].mean()
crew = (reg[reg.season.isin([2024, 2025])].groupby(["referee", "season"])["accepted"]
        .agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index())
wide = crew.pivot(index="referee", columns="season", values="mean").dropna().sort_values(2025)
n25 = crew[crew.season == 2025].set_index("referee")["size"].reindex(wide.index)
avg25 = reg[reg.season == 2025]["accepted"].mean()
sd_game = reg[reg.season == 2025]["accepted"].std()
se_crew = sd_game / np.sqrt(n25.mean())
S["pen25"] = f"{avg25:.1f}"
S["pen24"] = f"{by_season[2024]:.1f}"
S["pen_lo"], S["pen_hi"] = f"{by_season.min():.1f}", f"{by_season.max():.1f}"
S["crew_lo"], S["crew_hi"] = f"{wide[2025].min():.1f}", f"{wide[2025].max():.1f}"
S["crew_lo_name"], S["crew_hi_name"] = wide[2025].idxmin(), wide[2025].idxmax()
S["sd_game"] = f"{sd_game:.1f}"
S["se2"] = f"{2 * se_crew:.1f}"
S["ncrew"] = f"{len(wide)}"
S["r2425"] = f"{wide[2024].corr(wide[2025]):.2f}"
yy = []
cc = reg.groupby(["referee", "season"])["accepted"].mean().unstack()
for y in range(2016, 2025):
    d = cc[[y, y + 1]].dropna()
    yy.append(d[y].corr(d[y + 1]))
S["r_lo"], S["r_hi"] = f"{min(yy):.2f}", f"{max(yy):.2f}"
S["r_med"] = f"{np.median(yy):.2f}"
# share of crews whose 2024 rank half (top or bottom eight) held in 2025
top24 = wide[2024] > wide[2024].median()
top25 = wide[2025] > wide[2025].median()
S["same_half"] = f"{(top24 == top25).sum()}"

# --- replay reviews written into the play-by-play -----------------------------------------------
rv = raw[raw.replay_or_challenge == 1].copy()
ex = rv["desc"].str.extract(r"(challenged|Replay Official reviewed|Replay Assistant challenged|reviewed) "
                            r"the (.*?) ruling, and the play was (\w+)")
rv["who"] = np.where(ex[0].eq("challenged"), "challenge", np.where(ex[0].notna(), "booth", None))
rv["what"], rv["result"] = ex[1], ex[2].str.lower()
rv = rv[rv.who.notna()]
rv["reversed"] = rv["result"].eq("reversed")
ch = rv[(rv.who == "challenge") & (rv.season_type == "REG")]
ngames = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"].groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique()
S["ch_rate"] = f"{100 * ch.reversed.mean():.0f}%"
S["ch_rate24"] = f"{100 * ch[ch.season == 2024].reversed.mean():.0f}%"
S["ch_rate25"] = f"{100 * ch[ch.season == 2025].reversed.mean():.0f}%"
S["ch_pg25"] = f"{len(ch[ch.season == 2025]) / ngames[2025] / 2:.2f}"
S["ch_n25"] = f"{len(ch[ch.season == 2025])}"
S["g25"] = f"{ngames[2025]}"
recent = rv[rv.season.between(2021, 2025)]
S["rv_n"] = f"{len(recent):,}"
LABELS = {"pass completion": "Ruled a catch", "incomplete pass": "Ruled incomplete",
          "runner broke the plane": "Ruled a touchdown (broke the plane)",
          "short of the line to gain": "Spot: short of the line to gain", "first down": "Spot: ruled a first down",
          "fumble": "Ruled a fumble", "runner was not down by contact": "Ruled not down by contact",
          "interception": "Ruled an interception", "runner was down by contact": "Ruled down by contact",
          "short of the goal line": "Ruled short of the goal line",
          "runner was inbounds": "Ruled in bounds", "runner was out of bounds": "Ruled out of bounds"}
tab = (recent[recent.what.isin(LABELS)].groupby(["what", "who"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0))
tab["n"] = tab.sum(axis=1)
tab["rev"] = recent[recent.what.isin(LABELS)].groupby("what")["reversed"].mean()
tab = tab.sort_values("n")
S["catch_share"] = f"{100 * (tab.loc[['pass completion', 'incomplete pass'], 'n'].sum()) / len(recent):.0f}%"
S["plane_rev"] = f"{100 * tab.loc['runner broke the plane', 'rev']:.0f}%"
S["incomp_rev"] = f"{100 * tab.loc['incomplete pass', 'rev']:.0f}%"
S["catch_rev"] = f"{100 * tab.loc['pass completion', 'rev']:.0f}%"
```

Fourth quarter, 1:52 left in a one-score game. A receiver dives along the sideline, the ball pinned to his
chest, and tumbles out of bounds. The nearest official, a man in a black cap twenty yards downfield, waves
both arms across his body: incomplete. The home crowd roars at the stadium screen, which is replaying the
catch from a low angle. The losing coach grabs the red flag from his sock, then stops; he isn't allowed to
throw it. Thirty seconds later, with nobody on either sideline having asked, the official in the white cap
walks to the middle of the field, clicks on his microphone and says: *"After review, the ruling on the field
is reversed. The receiver had control of the ball with both feet down in bounds. The pass is complete."* Who
decided that? Why couldn't the coach challenge? And what exactly did "control with both feet down" have to
do with it? This chapter is about the people who run the game and the small set of rules that decide, on
almost every close play, who has the ball.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name the seven officials, find each one on a wide shot, and say which fouls he is most likely to throw a
  flag for.
- Say, for any close play, whether it can be reviewed and by whom: a coach's challenge, a booth review,
  replay assist, or nobody.
- Rule on a catch the way the replay official will (control, feet, then a football act), and say why the
  league rewrote the rule in 2018.
- Apply the rules of the ball: down by contact, forward progress, fumble versus incomplete pass, the fumble
  through the end zone, and backward versus forward passes.
- Call intentional grounding before the flag lands, using the tackle box and the line of scrimmage.
- Decode a referee's announcement and a virtual measurement, and predict "stands", "confirmed" or
  "reversed" before he says it.

## Seven officials, seven jobs

An NFL game is run by seven officials on the field, each wearing a number and a letter on his back that names
his job. A seven-person crew sounds like a lot until you count what happens on one snap: 22 players, most of
them in contact with someone, spread across 53 yards of width and, on a deep pass, 50 yards of depth, all in
about five seconds. Nobody can watch that. So the crew splits the field, and the players, into pieces. Each
official has a starting spot, a few players he is responsible for (his *keys*), an area he must cover once
the ball moves, and a short list of fouls that are his to call. The aim is that every player, every inch of
sideline and every goal line has at least one official looking at it, and the most important ones have two.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crew
#| fig-cap: "Where the seven officials stand before a snap (white discs; an 11-personnel offense in blue against a 4-3 defense in orange). Two officials work behind the offense: the referee (R), on the side of a right-handed quarterback's throwing arm, and the umpire (U) opposite him. Two straddle the line of scrimmage at the sidelines, just off the field: the down judge (DJ), on the side with the chain crew, and the line judge (LJ). Three work deep: the side judge (SJ) and field judge (FJ) about 20 yards downfield near each sideline, and the back judge (BJ) about 25 yards deep in the middle. Exact depths vary with the down, the distance and the formation."
off = offense("singleback")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-31.5, 31.5), window=(-16.5, 29.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
CREW = {  # key: (name, (d, w) of the official, (d, w) of his label)
    "R": ("Referee", (-12.0, 5.5), (-14.4, 5.5)),
    "U": ("Umpire", (-11.0, -5.5), (-13.4, -5.5)),
    "DJ": ("Down judge", (0.0, -28.4), (-2.6, -24.0)),
    "LJ": ("Line judge", (0.0, 28.4), (-2.6, 24.0)),
    "SJ": ("Side judge", (20.0, -23.5), (17.6, -23.5)),
    "FJ": ("Field judge", (20.0, 23.5), (17.6, 23.5)),
    "BJ": ("Back judge", (25.0, 4.0), (27.4, 4.0)),
}
for key, (name, (d, w), (ld, lw)) in CREW.items():
    official(ax, *XY(fld, p, d, w), key, ppy, r=1.25)
    say(fld, p, ld, lw, name, color=style.INK, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 10.0, -27.6, "sideline", fs=6.2, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, p, 10.0, 27.6, "sideline", fs=6.2, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, p, 1.4, 12.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, p, 11.4, -2.0, "line to gain", color=style.INK, fs=6.2)
marker_legend(ax)
plt.show()
```

Here is what each of them is watching. The table is the short version of the league's own description of
the positions;[^crew] the habits behind it are what let you guess who threw a flag before the referee says.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-crew
#| tbl-cap: "The seven officials: where they start, what they watch, and the calls you'll most often see them make."
rows = [
    ("**Referee** (R, white cap)", "Offensive backfield, 10–12 yards deep, on the quarterback's throwing-arm side",
     "The quarterback and the backs; the snap", "Roughing the passer, intentional grounding, fumble or pass by the quarterback; announces every foul and review"),
    ("**Umpire** (U)", "Offensive backfield opposite the referee; behind the defensive line near the goal line and late in each half",
     "The center, guards and the men across from them", "Holding (both sides) and false starts inside, illegal hands to the face; spots the ball; checks equipment"),
    ("**Down judge** (DJ)", "On the line of scrimmage at one sideline, with the chain crew",
     "The line (who's on it, who moved), the end and receivers on his side, his sideline",
     "Offside, encroachment, false start, illegal formation or motion; forward progress and out of bounds on his side"),
    ("**Line judge** (LJ)", "On the line of scrimmage at the other sideline",
     "The same as the down judge, on his side", "The same, plus whether a pass was thrown from beyond the line"),
    ("**Side judge** (SJ)", "About 20 yards deep near the down judge's sideline",
     "Receivers on his side once they're downfield", "Pass interference, illegal contact, catch or no catch, out of bounds"),
    ("**Field judge** (FJ)", "About 20 yards deep near the line judge's sideline",
     "Receivers on his side once they're downfield", "The same; under one upright on kicks"),
    ("**Back judge** (BJ)", "About 25 yards deep in the middle",
     "The tight end and inside receivers, the deep middle, the end line", "Deep pass interference, catches in the end zone; under the other upright on kicks"),
]
md_table(rows, ["Official", "Starts", "Watches", "Typical calls"], [":--", ":--", ":--", ":--"])
```

<!-- VERIFY: positions and depths in fig-crew and tbl-crew against the NFL's current "Officials' responsibilities and positions" page (referee 10-12 yd on the throwing-arm side; side/field judges ~20 yd; back judge ~25 yd). -->

A few things in that table explain a lot of what you see on Sundays.

**The wing officials own the line of scrimmage.** The down judge and line judge stand exactly on the line
at the sidelines so they can look straight down it. That is the only place from which you can see who is
offside, which receivers are on the line and which are off it (the
[formation rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) need seven on the
line), and whether a quarterback crossed the line before he threw. Most pre-snap fouls (the
[false starts and offsides](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)) come from these two. After the
snap they drift downfield along the sideline and mark where a runner's
[**forward progress**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-forward-progress) stopped: the spot you see an
official jog in and point his foot at.

**The umpire lives in the trenches, and he moved.** For most of football history the umpire stood
four or five yards behind the defensive line, in the middle of the linebackers, which is where the holding
happens. It was also where umpires kept getting run over. In 2010 the NFL moved him to the offensive
backfield, opposite the referee, where he watches the same linemen from behind.[^umpire] The trade was
visibility for safety: from behind you see a lineman's hands on a jersey less clearly. And it created a new
problem, because the umpire also spots the ball after most plays, and walking from the offensive backfield
to the ball slows the next snap. That is why he returns to his old spot behind the defense near the goal
line and in the final minutes of each half, when an offense wants to snap fast.
<!-- VERIFY: the umpire's current exceptions (inside the 5-yard line; final two minutes of the first half and final five of the second half) — the 2010 rule wording and any later change. -->

**The deep officials are pass officials.** The side judge, field judge and back judge are the reason a
deep throw can be judged at all. Each takes a share of the receivers, keeps them between himself and the
sideline or the end line, and rules on
[pass interference and illegal contact](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd), catches and out of bounds.
The seventh official, the side judge, was added in 1978, the same year the league loosened the rules on
pass defense to open up the passing game: more passing meant more eyes downfield.[^seventh]

**The referee is the boss, and the voice.** The referee wears the white cap and leads the crew. His spot,
behind and to the throwing-arm side of the quarterback, lets him watch the one player the rules protect
most: he is the official who throws most [roughing-the-passer](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd) flags,
and the one who decides whether a quarterback who lost the ball was throwing it or fumbling it. When a flag
lands, any official can have thrown it, but the crew gathers, the official who saw the foul tells the
referee what it was, and the referee announces it. A flag thrown by one official and waved off after the
conference ("picked up") usually means another official had a better look.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game a foul is a fact: the code knows a lineman held, and a flag appears. On a real field, a foul
exists only if an official in the right spot sees it. A hold on the far side of a run play can be in no
official's view, and a hold on the play side might be seen by two. That is why "they're letting them play"
is sometimes true, why the same contact draws a flag in front of the line judge and not behind the back of
the umpire, and why teams study which way each crew's eyes point. Officiating is a sample, not a census.
:::

### The crew in motion

Starting spots are only half of it. Watch a wide shot of a deep pass and you'll see the crew move as a
unit: the referee stays with the quarterback, the wing officials hold the line until the ball is thrown
(to see whether it was thrown from beyond it) and then run downfield, and the deep officials backpedal to
stay deeper and wider than the receivers they're judging, so that every catch is seen from the side or
from in front, never from behind.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crew-moves
#| fig-cap: "A deep pass seen through the officials (simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format; an illustrative play, not a real one). Snap: the crew in its starting spots. 1.2 s: the quarterback is in his drop and the receivers are climbing; the referee (R) watches the quarterback, the umpire (U) the linemen, and the down judge (DJ) and line judge (LJ) still hold the line, because only from there can they judge whether the pass was thrown from behind it. 2.6 s: the ball is thrown to the receiver on the right sideline; the wing officials release downfield and the field judge (FJ) backpedals to stay wider and deeper than the receiver. 4.7 s: the catch, judged by the field judge from in front and outside, with the line judge trailing to mark the spot. Faint lines are each person's path."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [q.moved(d=7.5) if q.key in ("LCB", "RCB") else q for q in dfn]
cm = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
cm.dropback(2.5)
cm.route("X", r.go(20)); cm.route("H", r.seam(18)); cm.route("Y", r.seam(18)); cm.route("Z", r.fade(26))
cm.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6.0), side=-1)
cm.pass_to("Z", t=2.6)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    cm.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)])
for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
    cm.rush(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
cm.drop("FS", (19.0, -10.0)); cm.drop("SS", (21.0, 11.5))
cm.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.5)); cm.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0)); cm.drop("NB", (9.0, -9.5))
cm.path("LCB", [(12.0, -1.5)]); cm.path("RCB", [(10.0, 2.6), (19.0, 2.4)])
trk = cm.to_tracking(t_after=1.6)
trk = trk[trk.time <= 4.8]
OFFICIALS = {
    "R": ("R", [(0, -12.0, 5.5), (1.0, -12.5, 6.5), (3.0, -12.0, 6.5), (4.6, -10.5, 7.5)]),
    "U": ("U", [(0, -11.0, -5.5), (1.0, -9.0, -5.0), (4.6, -8.5, -4.5)]),
    "DJ": ("DJ", [(0, 0.0, -28.4), (2.6, 0.0, -28.4), (4.6, 8.0, -28.4)]),
    "LJ": ("LJ", [(0, 0.0, 28.4), (2.6, 0.0, 28.4), (4.6, 12.0, 28.4)]),
    "SJ": ("SJ", [(0, 20.0, -23.5), (2.0, 23.5, -24.0), (4.6, 25.0, -23.5)]),
    "FJ": ("FJ", [(0, 20.0, 23.5), (1.6, 23.0, 24.0), (3.4, 29.5, 24.5), (4.6, 30.0, 24.0)]),
    "BJ": ("BJ", [(0, 25.0, 4.0), (2.4, 30.0, 4.5), (4.6, 32.0, 6.5)]),
}
NOTES = ["starting spots", "wings hold the line", "ball thrown: wings release", "the catch, seen from in front"]


def crew_notes(fld, i, t):
    lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
    fld.ax.set_title(f"{lab}: {NOTES[i]}", fontsize=8.2 if PDF else 10, color=style.INK, loc="left")


show_scene(cm, trk, [0.0, 1.2, 2.6, 4.7], window=(-16.0, 35.0), lateral=(-31.0, 31.0), extra=OFFICIALS,
           notes=crew_notes)
```

### Where the voice came from

The referee's microphone is younger than you might think. For most of the game's history fans learned what
a flag was for from the referee's arm signals and the next morning's newspaper. In 1975 the league's
supervisor of officials, Art McNally, put wireless microphones on referees so they could tell the stadium,
and the television audience, what had been called. McNally, a former high-school and college official from
Philadelphia who ran NFL officiating from 1968 to 1990, spent his career trying to make officiating
explainable: he also championed the first instant-replay system in 1986, and the league's officiating
command center in New York is named after him. In 2022 he became the first official elected to the Pro
Football Hall of Fame.[^mcnally]

## Replay: three doors into the booth

Officials miss things; they are watching a five-second play at full speed from one angle. Replay exists to
fix the misses that matter most without stopping the game every few minutes, and the NFL's answer is a
system with three separate doors, each with its own rules about who may open it and what it can change.

First, the history, because each door was added to fix a problem the last one created.[^replayhist]

- **1986–1991: the first try.** An official in the press box could stop the game to review a play. There
  were no challenges. The system was slow, overturned little, and was voted out after 1991.
- **1999: the challenge flag.** Replay came back with a twist: the *coaches* would decide which plays to
  review, by throwing a red flag, and pay for a failed challenge with a timeout. The booth kept control of the
  final two minutes of each half, so coaches couldn't use challenges as free timeouts when the clock matters
  most.
- **2011 and 2012: automatic reviews.** Every scoring play (2011) and every turnover (2012) became a booth
  review, so a coach no longer had to spend a challenge to fix the biggest calls of the game.
- **2017: New York decides.** The final say moved from the referee under a sideline hood to the league's
  senior officiating staff in New York, with the referee consulting on a tablet, so that the same handful of
  people judge every review in every game.
- **2019: the pass-interference experiment.** After a missed interference call decided the NFC
  Championship Game in January 2019 (the story is in
  [Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd)), pass interference was reviewable for
  one season. Almost nothing was overturned, and the experiment was dropped.
- **2020s: replay assist.** The booth began fixing clear-cut objective facts on its own, without a formal
  stop, and its powers grew in 2025 and 2026 (below).

Every review uses the same standard: the ruling on the field is changed only on **clear and obvious**
visual evidence. That produces the three outcomes in every announcement. *Reversed* means the video shows
the call was wrong. *Confirmed* means the video shows it was right. *Stands* means the video doesn't show
enough either way, so the call on the field survives. The distinction matters for your predictions: on a
play the camera can't see well (a ball at the bottom of a pile, a knee hidden by a body), the answer is
almost always "stands", whatever the call was.

### Door 1: the coach's challenge

A [**coach's challenge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coach-s-challenge) is the head coach asking for a
review by throwing a red flag onto the field before the next snap. The rules make it scarce on purpose:[^challenges]

- Each team gets **two challenges** a game. Since 2024 it gets **a third if either of the first two
  succeeds**; before that, both had to succeed.
- A team must have a **timeout** left to challenge, and it **loses that timeout if the challenge fails**.
- A coach may not challenge in the **final two minutes of either half** or in **overtime**, or challenge a
  play the booth reviews automatically (a scoring play or a turnover); those belong to the booth.
- Only certain rulings are reviewable: whether a pass was caught, whether a runner was down, in bounds or
  across the goal line, the spot relative to the line to gain or the goal line, who recovered a loose ball,
  too many men on the field. Judgment fouls, holding or interference, are not.

Why make it expensive? Because a free challenge would be thrown on every close play, and each review costs
two or three minutes of everyone's time. The timeout charge turns a challenge into a bet: throw the flag
when the expected gain (the chance of winning the review times what the reversal is worth) beats the
expected cost (the chance of losing times what a timeout is worth later). That is exactly the kind of
decision the [game-management staff](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) upstairs exists to
make, often in the eight or ten seconds before the next snap, with a video coordinator watching the
television replay and calling the head coach's headset. It's also why an offense that likes the call
on the field hurries to the line: once the ball is snapped, the play can't be challenged
([In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)).

And it's why challenges are rarer than you'd guess. In 2025 coaches threw `{python} S["ch_n25"]` challenges in
`{python} S["g25"]` regular-season games, about `{python} S["ch_pg25"]` per team per game, and won
`{python} S["ch_rate25"]` of them; over 2016–2025 the success rate was `{python} S["ch_rate"]`.[^reviewcalc]
A coach who is right about half the time, and is only betting on plays he's fairly sure of, is telling you
how hard it is to see a play clearly from the sideline in ten seconds.

### Door 2: booth review

A [**booth review**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-booth-review) is started by the replay official in the
stadium, working with the league's officiating command center, not by a coach. It covers:

- **every scoring play** (touchdowns, field goals, safeties) and **every try**;
- **every turnover** (interceptions, fumbles recovered by the defense, and muffed kicks recovered by the
  kicking team);
- **every reviewable play in the final two minutes of each half and in overtime**.

Most booth reviews never stop the game. A touchdown is looked at during the celebration and the try is lined
up; if the video agrees, the game goes on. If the booth wants a closer look, it signals the referee (the
officials wear a buzzer for this) and the game stops. The coach's flag is irrelevant here: the booth decides
whether to look. A [**replay review**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-replay-review) of either kind ends
the same way, with the referee walking to the middle of the field, turning on his microphone, and reading
New York's decision.

### Door 3: replay assist

The newest door is the quietest. [**Replay assist**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-replay-assist) lets the
booth tell the on-field crew about a clear-cut objective fact while the officials are still sorting out the
play, with no formal review and usually no stoppage you'd notice: the ball was actually spotted a yard short,
the runner's knee was down before the ball came out, the receiver's second foot landed out of bounds, two
seconds should go back on the clock. It began in the early 2020s as a way to fix the obvious without a coach
having to gamble a timeout on it.
<!-- VERIFY: the year replay assist was first used (curriculum says 2023; other reports date the booth's objective-fact "assist" to 2021-2022). -->

In 2025 the league gave it its first power over fouls. Replay assist may now **overturn** a flag for a hit on
a defenseless player, a face mask, a horse-collar tackle, tripping, or roughing or running into the kicker,
when the video plainly shows the foul didn't happen (the hand never touched the face mask, the kicker was
never touched). It **cannot add** a foul that nobody called. In 2026 the league added one more: its
officiating staff may **consult** with the on-field crew on ejections for flagrant football acts and
non-football acts, such as a punch thrown away from the play. Some reports describe that as replay ejecting
players on its own; the league's official wording is only that it may consult.[^assist]

What the NFL still doesn't have is a **sky judge**: an official in the booth with the power to call or wipe
out any foul, in real time, the way a video referee works in some other sports. Other leagues have tried
versions of it, and the NFL has discussed it for years. The objections are practical: it would slow the
game, it would turn every play (on which, coaches like to say, somebody is holding) into a candidate for a
flag, and it would put judgment calls in the hands of someone watching a screen rather than the field. So
the league has expanded replay one narrow, objective slice at a time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-replay-doors
#| fig-cap: "Who can review a close call, as of the 2026 season. Read from the top: plays the booth reviews automatically come first, and only plays that fall through to the second question can be challenged by a coach. Replay assist works alongside both, on clear objective facts and on flags for a short list of fouls, usually without stopping the game. Judgment fouls such as holding and pass interference can't be reviewed at all."
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 6.0)
Q, A_B, A_C, A_R, A_N = "#efeee9", style.OFFENSE_TINT, style.DEFENSE_TINT, "#d4efe5", "#f3f2ee"
qx, ax_ = 30, 78
fbox(ax, 50, 88.5, 56, 6.5, "A close call on the field", fc=Q, tfs=8.4)
qs = [
    (74.0, "Scoring play, turnover or try?\nOr inside 2:00 of a half, or overtime?"),
    (54.0, "A reviewable ruling? (catch, down,\nin or out of bounds, the spot at the line\nto gain or goal line, a recovery)"),
    (34.0, "An objective fact the booth can see at\nonce, or a flag for one of the five\nlisted fouls?"),
    (14.0, "A flagrant act that may\nmean an ejection?"),
]
outs = [
    ("BOOTH REVIEW", "automatic: the replay official\nstops play if he wants a closer look;\nNew York decides", A_B, style.OFFENSE),
    ("COACH'S CHALLENGE", "red flag before the next snap;\ncosts a timeout if it fails;\n2 a game, a 3rd if either wins", A_C, style.DEFENSE),
    ("REPLAY ASSIST", "booth tells the crew, usually\nno stoppage; can wipe out a\nlisted flag, never add one", A_R, GREEN),
    ("CONSULT (2026)", "league officiating staff may\nadvise the referee on\nan ejection", A_N, style.BASELINE),
]
farrow(ax, (qx, 85.2), (qx, 80.3))
for i, ((y, qtext), (t, b, fc, ec)) in enumerate(zip(qs, outs)):
    fbox(ax, qx, y, 50, 12.0 if i < 3 else 10.0, qtext, fc=Q, tfs=7.0)
    fbox(ax, ax_, y, 38, 13.0, t, b, fc=fc, ec=ec, tfs=7.6, bfs=6.5)
    farrow(ax, (qx + 25.2, y), (ax_ - 19.2, y), "yes", toff=(0, 1.8))
    if i < 3:
        farrow(ax, (qx, y - 6.1), (qx, qs[i + 1][0] + (6.1 if i < 2 else 5.1)), "no", toff=(3.2, 0))
farrow(ax, (qx, 8.9), (qx, 5.4), "no", toff=(3.2, 0.2))
ax.text(5.0, 3.0, "The call on the field is final (holding, pass interference, most fouls).", ha="left",
        va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", transform=ax.transData,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc=A_N, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8))
plt.show()
```

### What actually gets reviewed

Play-by-play data records a review whenever one changes or stops the game, with the ruling that was
reviewed and the result, so you can see where replay earns its keep.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reviews
#| fig-cap: "The twelve rulings reviewed most often, 2021–2025 (regular season and playoffs), split by who asked: a coach's challenge (orange) or the booth (blue). The label gives the share of those reviews that reversed the call. Catch or no catch is by far the busiest question. Reversal rates look high for booth reviews such as 'broke the plane' because the play-by-play generally records a booth review only when it stopped the game, not the routine quick confirmations of every touchdown. Source: nflverse play-by-play (the review text in each play's description)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
ys = np.arange(len(tab))
ax.barh(ys, tab["challenge"], color=style.DEFENSE, height=0.62, label="Coach's challenge")
ax.barh(ys, tab["booth"], left=tab["challenge"], color=style.OFFENSE, height=0.62, label="Booth review")
for y, (_, row) in zip(ys, tab.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row.n + 6, y, f"{100 * row.rev:.0f}% reversed", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.9,
            color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [LABELS[k] for k in tab.index], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlim(0, tab["n"].max() * 1.32)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Reviews, 2021–2025", fontsize=7.6)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two patterns are worth carrying into a game. First, catch-or-no-catch rulings make up about
`{python} S["catch_share"]` of all the recorded reviews, which is why the next section spends so long on the
catch. Second, the direction of the call matters. A pass ruled *incomplete* was reversed `{python} S["incomp_rev"]`
of the time and one ruled a *catch* `{python} S["catch_rev"]`; officials are taught that when in doubt, they
should let the play run and rule a catch or a fumble, because replay can take a catch away cleanly, but
can't easily invent what would have happened after a whistle (more on that in a moment).

## The catch

Nothing in the rulebook has caused more arguments than the definition of a catch, and the reason is the
stakes. Whether a pass was caught decides more than one play. If it was a catch and the ball then comes
loose, it's a **fumble**: a live ball anyone can recover. If it wasn't, it's an **incomplete pass**: the ball
is dead and the offense keeps it. A single definition separates "the offense keeps the ball and loses a
down" from "the defense may have it". So the rule has to draw a line between *possessing* a ball and merely
*touching* it, at full speed, in the air, often while someone is hitting the receiver.

Today's rule, rewritten in 2018, says a player has made a
[**catch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-catch-completed-pass) when, in bounds, he does three things in
order:[^catchrule]

1. **Control.** He secures control of the ball in his hands or arms before it touches the ground.
2. **Feet (or a body part) down.** He touches the ground in bounds with both feet, or with any part of his
   body other than his hands (a knee, a hip, an elbow).
3. **Time.** After the first two, he makes an *act common to the game*: tucks the ball away, turns upfield,
   takes an extra step, reaches the ball toward the line, wards off a defender. Or he keeps control long
   enough that he *could* have.

Two clarifications do most of the work on replays. A ball that moves slightly in his hands while he keeps
control is still controlled. And the ground can't help him: if he goes to the ground before he has finished
step 3, he must keep control when he lands. If the ball pops loose and touches the ground before step 3, the
pass is incomplete; if it pops loose after step 3, it was a catch and then a fumble. An interception is
judged by exactly the same three steps.

```{python}
#| label: fig-catch
#| fig-cap: "The catch rule as a replay official applies it (NFL rule since 2018). A pass must pass all three gates in order. Failing gate 1 or 2 means incomplete; the ball coming loose before gate 3 means incomplete; losing it after gate 3 means a catch and then a fumble. The same test decides an interception."
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 5.6)
G, YES, NO = "#efeee9", "#d4efe5", "#fbe3e1"
cx, rx = 34, 82
fbox(ax, cx, 81, 46, 6.0, "The pass arrives", fc=G, tfs=8.2)
gates = [
    (67, "1. Control", "secured in his hands or arms\nbefore the ball touches the ground?"),
    (49, "2. Feet down in bounds", "both feet, or any body part\nother than his hands?"),
    (31, "3. Time", "an act common to the game (tuck, turn\nupfield, extra step, reach, ward off),\nor control long enough to make one?"),
]
farrow(ax, (cx, 77.9), (cx, 73.6))
for i, (y, t, b) in enumerate(gates):
    fbox(ax, cx, y, 46, 12.6, t, b, fc=G, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.6)
    nxt = gates[i + 1][0] + 6.4 if i < 2 else 17.4
    farrow(ax, (cx, y - 6.4), (cx, nxt), "yes", toff=(3.4, 0))
fbox(ax, rx, 67, 28, 10.5, "INCOMPLETE", "a bobble, or the ball\nhit the ground first", fc=NO, ec=RED)
fbox(ax, rx, 49, 28, 10.5, "INCOMPLETE", "out of bounds (in the\nend zone: no touchdown)", fc=NO, ec=RED)
fbox(ax, rx, 31, 28, 12.5, "STILL GOING", "keeps control through the\nground or out of bounds,\nor it's incomplete", fc="#fdf3d8",
     ec=style.LINE_TO_GAIN)
for y in (67, 49):
    farrow(ax, (cx + 23.2, y), (rx - 14.2, y), "no", toff=(0, 1.9))
farrow(ax, (cx + 23.2, 31), (rx - 14.2, 31), "not yet", toff=(0, 1.9))
fbox(ax, cx, 11, 46, 12.0, "CATCH", "if the ball comes loose now: a fumble\n(live ball). If he's in the end zone,\nor reaches it over the line: touchdown", fc=YES,
     ec=GREEN, tfs=8.6)
fbox(ax, rx, 8.5, 28, 11.0, "Slight movement", "of the ball in his hands\nwith control kept is not\na loss of control", fc=G, tfs=7.2, bfs=6.4)
farrow(ax, (rx - 4, 24.7), (cx + 23.4, 14.5), "keeps it", toff=(1.5, 1.6))
plt.show()
```

### Why the rule was rewritten

For most of the 2010s the rule had an extra clause that produced some of the most hated rulings in league
history. A receiver who went to the ground "in the process of the catch" had to keep control of the ball
*after* hitting the ground, the so-called *survive the ground* requirement, no matter how many steps he had
taken or how obviously he had possessed it. The clause was meant to make the rule objective: instead of
asking officials to judge whether a player had possession long enough, it gave them a test they could see on
video. The trouble was that the objective test kept ruling against what everyone watching had seen. Three
plays made it untenable:[^catchhist]

- **Calvin Johnson, Lions at Bears, September 12, 2010.** Trailing 19–14 with 31 seconds left, Johnson
  caught a pass in the end zone, landed with both feet and his backside, and put the ball down on the turf
  as he rolled to get up. Ruled incomplete; the booth upheld it. The Lions lost by five, and "the Calvin
  Johnson rule" entered the vocabulary.
- **Dez Bryant, Cowboys at Packers, divisional playoffs, January 11, 2015.** Fourth-and-2 at the Green Bay
  32, 4:42 left, Dallas trailing 26–21. Tony Romo threw deep down the left sideline; Bryant caught it, took
  three steps as he fell and reached the ball toward the goal line, and it touched the ground and moved
  as he landed at the 1. Ruled a catch on the field, reversed on Green Bay's challenge. The Packers ran out
  the clock and won 26–21.
- **Jesse James, Patriots at Steelers, December 17, 2017.** With 34 seconds left and Pittsburgh down
  27–24, James caught a pass at the 10, went to a knee, and lunged across the goal line; the ball moved
  as it hit the turf. Ruled a touchdown, reversed by the booth. The Steelers lost the game and, as it
  turned out, home-field advantage in the playoffs.

The league's competition committee rewrote the rule that offseason. The 2018 version deleted the
going-to-the-ground clause and replaced the old "football move" with the plainer "act common to the game",
and the league's officiating chiefs said publicly that under it, Bryant's and James's catches would have
counted: reaching the ball toward the goal line is a football act.
<!-- VERIFY: the league (Troy Vincent / Al Riveron, March 2018) saying the Bryant and James plays would be catches under the 2018 rule. -->

The trade-off is worth naming, because it's the same trade the whole replay system keeps making. The old
rule was objective and produced absurd results; the new rule matches what people see, at the price of a
judgment call ("did he have time?") at the center of it. Disputes didn't disappear; they moved from "did
the ball move when he hit the ground?" to "was that lunge a football act or part of the fall?"

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The ball touched the ground, so it's incomplete." The ball is allowed to touch the ground during a catch,
as long as the receiver keeps control of it, with his hands under it or the ball pinned to his body. What it
can't do is help him: a ball trapped against the turf with no hand under it, or one that pops loose when he
lands before he has finished the catch, is incomplete.
:::

### Sidelines and end zones

Two places put extra weight on gate 2. At the **sideline**, a receiver needs both feet (or another body
part) down in bounds with control; one foot, as in college football, isn't enough. Since 2008 there has been
no "force-out" ruling either: a receiver pushed out of bounds in the air before getting both feet down has
not caught the ball, however sure the official is that he would have landed in bounds.[^forceout] And
because a toe-tap catch leaves no time for a football act before he goes out of bounds, he must keep control
as he falls out; a ball jarred loose when he hits the ground out of bounds is incomplete.

In the **end zone**, the catch is the touchdown, so the receiver must complete all three steps there. That
is different from a runner who already has the ball: for him, the ball only has to touch the plane of the
goal line (the [end zone](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) is generous that way).
Under the 2018 rule, a receiver who completes the catch short of the goal line and then reaches the ball
across it has scored, which is exactly what Jesse James did.

## Down, progress and the whistle

A play ends when the ball becomes dead, and most of the time that means a ball carrier going down. The NFL's
definition is different from the one you may know from college. A runner is
[**down by contact**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-by-contact) when any part of his body other than
his hands or feet touches the ground *after he has been touched by an opponent*. If nobody touched him, he
isn't down: a running back who slips on wet turf, or a returner who kneels to field a bouncing kick, may get
up and keep running. In college football the runner is down as soon as his knee touches, contact or
not.[^downrule] (A runner who slides feet-first or simply gives himself up is down where he does it; that's
how quarterbacks protect themselves.)

The order of events matters more than anything else on these plays. If the ball comes out *before* the knee
(or elbow, or hip) touches after contact, it's a fumble: live, and anyone's. If the knee touches first, the
runner was down and the ball coming out afterward doesn't matter. On television these are separated by a
few frames of video, which is why they're among the most-reviewed rulings in the data above.

```{python}
#| label: fig-down-fumble
#| fig-cap: "Down or fumble? It depends on the order of three events: the defender's contact, the ball coming loose, and the runner's knee (or any body part other than a hand or foot) touching the ground. Top: the ball comes out first, so it's a fumble and the ball is live. Middle: the knee touches first, after contact, so he's down and the play is dead before the ball comes loose. Bottom: nobody touched him, so in the NFL he isn't down; he can get up and keep running (in college he'd be down)."
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 2.3, xmax=100, ymax=36)
rows = [
    (26.0, [(10, "contact"), (31, "ball comes out"), (52, "knee down")], "FUMBLE", "live ball: anyone may recover", RED),
    (16.0, [(10, "contact"), (31, "knee down"), (52, "ball comes out")], "DOWN", "dead at the spot of the knee", GREEN),
    (6.0, [(10, "slips, untouched"), (31, "knee down"), (52, "gets up, runs on")], "NOT DOWN", "NFL: still live (college: down)", style.OFFENSE_DARK),
]
ax.text(3, 33.4, "time →", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
for y, evs, verdict, sub, col in rows:
    ax.plot([3, 62], [y, y], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
    for i, (x, lab) in enumerate(evs):
        ax.plot(x, y, marker="o", ms=7, color=col if i == 1 else style.INK_2, zorder=3)
        ax.text(x, y + 2.6, lab, fontsize=6.9, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=4)
    ax.text(66, y + 1.3, verdict, fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=col, ha="left", va="center")
    ax.text(66, y - 1.6, sub, fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
plt.show()
```

**Forward progress** decides *where* the play ended. You met it in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd): the
ball is spotted at the farthest point it reached toward the goal line before the runner was stopped, not
where he ended up after a pile drove him back. The same idea tells officials when to blow the whistle. A
runner wrapped up and held upright, his legs still churning, has had his forward progress stopped even
though he hasn't gone down, and the officials will whistle the play dead rather than let a pile of
defenders keep shoving him backward (or strip the ball from a man who has stopped moving forward). It also
protects runners at the goal line: a back who gets the ball across the plane and is then knocked back
into the field has scored. And on a screen it protects a quarterback in a different way, because a
quarterback dropping back on his own is spotted where he goes down; only being *driven* back is undone.

### The whistle, and the 2008 lesson

The whistle is the one tool officials can't take back. Once it blows, the play is dead, whatever happens
next. That used to put replay in an impossible position: if an official ruled a play over (an incomplete
pass, a runner down) and the video showed a fumble, replay could fix the ruling but could not know who would
have recovered the ball if everyone had kept playing.

The play that made everyone face this came on September 14, 2008. Denver trailed San Diego 38–31 with 1:17
left, second-and-goal at the 1. Jay Cutler dropped back, and the ball slipped out of his hand as he started
to throw; a Charger fell on it. Referee Ed Hochuli ruled it an incomplete pass and blew his whistle. Replay
showed a fumble, but because the whistle had already killed the play, the Chargers couldn't be given the
ball; Denver kept it at the spot of the fumble, scored two plays later, went for two, and won 39–38.[^hochuli]
Hochuli, one of the most respected referees of his era, publicly apologized.

Two things changed. The rules now let replay award the ball to the team that recovered it when the recovery
is clear and in the *immediate continuing action*, even after a whistle. And the officials' habit changed:
on a bang-bang fumble, they are taught to hold the whistle, let the players finish the scramble for the
ball, and rule a fumble when in doubt, because replay can turn a fumble back into a dead ball cleanly but
can't recreate a recovery that never happened. That is why you now see plays continue for a few seconds after
a runner seems to be down, and a defender scooping up a loose ball and running the other way while
everyone else has stopped.
<!-- VERIFY: the year (2009?) and wording of the replay change allowing a clear recovery in the immediate continuing action to be awarded after an incorrect incomplete/down ruling. -->

## Pass or fumble: the quarterback's arm

A close cousin of down-or-fumble is pass-or-fumble, and it comes up every time a pass rusher hits a
quarterback as he throws. The rule is about the arm. Once the quarterback, holding the ball, starts his arm
moving forward to throw, anything that comes out is a forward pass, and if it hits the ground it's
incomplete. If he loses the ball *before* his arm starts forward, or while he is pulling it back down
to tuck it after deciding not to throw, it's a fumble.

The second half of that sentence was not always true. Until 2013 the rulebook had the **tuck rule**: if the
quarterback started forward and then brought the ball back toward his body, it was still a pass until he
had tucked it all the way in. It is remembered for one snowy night in Foxborough: the divisional playoff in
January 2002, when Tom Brady lost the ball under a hit from Charles Woodson late in the fourth quarter, the
Raiders recovered, and replay applied the tuck rule to call it an incomplete pass. New England kept the
ball, tied the game with a field goal and won in overtime, the first playoff run of a dynasty. The league
abolished the rule in 2013.[^tuck] Today the same play is a fumble.

Because these are turnovers when ruled fumbles, the booth reviews every one of them. When you see a
strip-sack ruled on the field, watch the arm, not the ball: if the arm was coming forward with the ball in
the hand, expect "reversed, incomplete pass".

## A fumble through the end zone

Now the harshest rule in the book. When a fumble goes out of bounds, the general rule is generous to the
team that fumbled: it keeps the ball. If the ball went out going backward, it's spotted where it went out;
if it went out going *forward*, it comes back to the spot of the fumble, so that nobody gains yards by
fumbling forward on purpose.

The exception is the opponent's end zone. A
[**fumble through the end zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fumble-through-the-end-zone-touchback),
a ball fumbled forward into the end zone that goes out of bounds there, out the side or out the back, is a
**touchback**: the defense gets the ball at its own 20, even though no defender ever touched it.[^fumbleoob]

```{python}
#| label: fig-fumble-oob
#| fig-cap: "Three fumbles out of bounds near the goal line, offense moving up the page. Left: the ball squirts forward and out at the 2: the offense keeps it, but back at the 4, the spot of the fumble, because a forward fumble can't gain ground. Middle: knocked loose at the 1, it bounces into the end zone and out the side: a touchback, and the defense takes over at its own 20. Right: the ball goes backward and out at the 8: the offense keeps it where it went out. The X marks the fumble, the dashed brown line the ball's path."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
cases = [
    ((-2.0, 18.0), (2.0, 19.2), [(2.0, 19.2), (3.2, 21.4), (4.0, 23.58), (4.3, 24.8)], "offense's ball\nat the 4", (3.4, 13.5), style.OFFENSE_DARK),
    ((-1.5, 18.5), (5.0, 21.0), [(5.0, 21.0), (7.8, 22.4), (11.5, 23.58), (12.2, 24.8)], "touchback:\ndefense's ball\nat its 20", (11.6, 14.2), RED),
    ((-1.0, 16.5), (2.0, 19.5), [(2.0, 19.5), (0.5, 21.6), (-2.0, 23.58), (-2.6, 24.8)], "offense's ball\nat the 8", (-4.6, 15.5), style.OFFENSE_DARK),
]
for ax, (start, fum, ballpath, verdict, vat, col) in zip(axes, cases):
    rb = O("RB", "RB", start[0], start[1], "R")
    q = Play([rb], [D("DB", "DB", fum[0] + 0.9, fum[1] + 1.1, "D")], los=104, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
    q.run("RB", [fum], absolute=True)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(7.0, 29.5), window=(-6.5, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    say(fld, q, 2.0, 26.6, "out of bounds", fs=5.6, box=False, rot=90)
    for dd, lab in ((1.0, "5"), (-4.0, "10")):
        say(fld, q, dd + 0.6, 9.0, lab, fs=5.8, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
    xmark(fld, q, *fum)
    path_arrow(fld, q, ballpath)
    say(fld, q, vat[0], vat[1], verdict, color=col, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
    say(fld, q, 6.0, 12.0, "goal line", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
    say(fld, q, 14.4, 11.0, "end line", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
for ax, lab in zip(axes, ["Forward, out at the 2", "Into the end zone, out", "Backward, out at the 8"]):
    ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=7.8, color=style.INK, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

Why would the rules punish the offense so hard? The logic is about territory, not possession. The end zone
belongs to the defending team. When a ball goes dead in or behind your end zone because of something the
other team did (a punt rolls through, a kickoff sails out the back), the result is a touchback, your ball
at your 20, like the [touchbacks on punts](09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd). A fumble into your end zone and
out is treated the same way: the offense put the ball there, it died there, and it's yours. The rule is
consistent; it just doesn't feel fair, because the offense had the ball a moment earlier and the defense
did nothing to earn it. It is one of the most criticized rules in the book, and proposals to soften it
(giving the ball back to the offense at the spot of the fumble, say) have been floated without becoming
the rule.
<!-- VERIFY: recent competition-committee or team proposals to change the fumble-through-the-end-zone touchback, and that none has passed through 2026. -->

The rule shapes technique. It's why coaches drill runners and receivers to carry the ball in the arm away
from the defenders near the goal line, why a ball carrier stretching for the pylon is taking a real gamble,
and why defenders near the goal line punch at the ball instead of wrapping up. A clean tackle at the 1 gives
the offense first-and-goal; a punched ball through the end zone gives the defense the ball at the 20.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the fourth-down fumble rule"}
One more fumble rule has a famous origin. On September 10, 1978, with the Raiders trailing the Chargers in
the final seconds, Ken Stabler, about to be sacked, fumbled the ball forward; teammates batted and kicked it
toward the goal line, and Dave Casper fell on it in the end zone for the winning touchdown. The "Holy
Roller" was legal then. The next season the league made it impossible: on fourth down, and on any down after
the two-minute warning, only the player who fumbled may recover and advance the ball. If a teammate
recovers it, the ball comes back to the spot of the fumble (or the spot of recovery, if that is behind
it).[^holyroller] The rule exists to stop an offense from fumbling forward on purpose when it has nothing
left to lose.
:::

## Backward passes and forward passes

Football allows exactly **one forward pass per play**, and it must be thrown from behind the line of
scrimmage. It allows any number of [**backward passes**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-backward-pass)
(also called [**laterals**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-lateral)), from anywhere, by anyone, at any
time. The two are treated very differently when they hit the ground:

- A **forward pass** that hits the ground is **incomplete**. The ball is dead, and the offense keeps it.
- A **backward pass** that hits the ground is **still live**, exactly like a fumble. Either team may recover
  it, and either team may advance it.

Which is which? The test is the ball's direction: compare the yard line where it left the passer's hand
with the yard line where it is first touched (or first hits the ground). If the second is closer to the
opponent's goal, the pass was forward. If it's the same yard line or behind, the pass was backward, so a
pass thrown perfectly parallel to the line counts as **backward**.[^lateral] Notice that it's the ball's
path that counts, not the players' positions on the field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lateral
#| fig-cap: "Forward or backward is decided by the yard line where the ball leaves the passer's hand (dashed 'release line') and the yard line where it's first touched. From the shotgun, the quarterback catches the snap five yards deep. A pitch to the running back (1) goes behind the release line: a backward pass, live if it hits the ground. A bubble screen (2) caught after the slot receiver has bowed back to the release line is parallel, which counts as backward. A quick screen to the outside receiver (3) is caught four yards ahead of the release line: a forward pass, incomplete (and dead) if it's dropped."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q.moved(d=-6.5, w=6.0) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off]
off = [q.moved(d=-5.5, w=-8.5) if q.key == "H" else q for q in off]
lp = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=None)
fld = lp.draw(lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-12.0, 4.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
rel = (-5.4, 0.3)
x0, y0 = XY(fld, lp, rel[0], -18.5)
x1, y1 = XY(fld, lp, rel[0], 18.5)
ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)
say(fld, lp, -4.6, -14.3, "release line", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
for tgt, num, col, lab, lat in [((-6.6, 5.0), "1", GREEN, "1  backward:\nlive if dropped", (-9.2, 6.6)),
                                ((-5.4, -7.5), "2", GREEN, "2  parallel = backward:\nlive if dropped", (-8.6, -10.0)),
                                ((-0.9, 14.2), "3", RED, "3  forward:\nincomplete if dropped", (1.9, 9.6))]:
    path_arrow(fld, lp, [rel, tgt], color=style.BALL, lw=1.5)
    say(fld, lp, lat[0], lat[1], lab, color=col, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
say(fld, lp, 1.0, -2.5, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
plt.show()
```

Why does a dropped backward pass stay live? Because otherwise the backward pass would be a free way to move
the ball sideways with no risk, and the rules want risk to come with that freedom. The result shows up in
three places on a broadcast:

- **Pitches and option plays.** A pitch on the
  [option](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) is a backward pass. Drop it and you've fumbled, in
  effect, which is why option teams drill the pitch relentlessly.
- **Screens.** Most screens thrown from the shotgun are forward passes, because the quarterback releases
  the ball five or six yards behind the line and the receiver catches it closer to the line than that. But
  a bubble or swing screen to a player who has drifted back level with the quarterback may be backward, and
  a defender who sees it hit the ground should pick it up and run. Coaches teach defenders to scoop up every
  loose screen and let the officials sort it out. The rules on linemen downfield follow the same line: the
  [illegal-man-downfield rule](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) applies only when a forward pass is
  thrown beyond the line, so on a true backward pass linemen may already be blocking downfield.
- **Last-play desperation.** The multi-lateral kickoff return or final snap, the ball pitched backward
  again and again, is legal because every pitch is backward.

The most famous backward pass in NFL history came in a wild-card game on January 8, 2000. Buffalo had just
kicked a go-ahead field goal with 16 seconds left. On the kickoff, Tennessee's Lorenzo Neal handed the ball
to tight end Frank Wycheck, who turned and threw it across the field to Kevin Dyson, who ran 75 yards
untouched down the sideline for the winning touchdown. Replay looked at whether Wycheck's throw had gone
forward. It hadn't been shown to: the ruling of a legal lateral stood, and the "Music City Miracle" became
the standard illustration of the rule that what counts is the ball's path from hand to hands.[^musiccity]

## Intentional grounding and the tackle box

[Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) introduced the
[throwaway](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-throwaway) and the rule that limits it. Here is the full rule,
and the reasoning behind it.

[**Intentional grounding**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding) is a foul when a passer
who is facing an imminent loss of yardage because of the rush throws a pass that isn't in the direction and
vicinity of an originally eligible receiver. Three conditions, all needed:[^grounding]

1. **Pressure.** He must be facing a likely sack. A quarterback under no pressure who throws the ball into
   the turf has wasted a down, but he hasn't grounded it.
2. **No realistic target.** The pass isn't thrown near an eligible receiver. "Near" is a judgment, and
   throwing the ball well over the head of a covered receiver in the right part of the field counts.
3. **Inside the tackle box.** The [**tackle box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box), which the
   rulebook calls the *pocket area*, is the region between the outside edges of where the two offensive
   tackles lined up, running from the line of scrimmage all the way back to the offense's own end line.

The exception is what makes the box matter: **a passer who is or has been outside the tackle box may throw
the ball away freely, as long as it lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage** (extended to the sidelines),
including out of bounds past it. Since the 2024 rulebook he counts as outside the box if any part of his
body, or the ball, is outside it. And "has been" means what it says: a quarterback who escapes the box and
then drifts back inside it keeps the exception for the rest of the play.

The penalty is built to cost about what the sack would have: **loss of down and 10 yards** from the previous
spot, or loss of down at the spot of the pass if that is farther back, and **a safety** if he throws it
from his own end zone. The other exception you'll see every week is the **spike**: a quarterback who throws
the ball straight into the ground immediately after taking the snap, to stop the clock, isn't penalized;
it costs a down and nothing else. Spikes belong to the end-of-half clock game, which is in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: fig-tackle-box
#| fig-cap: "Intentional grounding backed up at the offense's own 4, where the tackle box (shaded) runs back into the end zone. Quarterback A, inside the box and in his end zone, throws to an empty part of the field (1): grounding, and from the end zone that's a safety. Throwing it over the covered tight end's head instead (2) is a legal throwaway. Quarterback B has escaped the box: throwing it out of bounds past the line of scrimmage (3) is legal even though no one is near, but a throw that lands out of bounds short of the line (4) is grounding, also a safety from the end zone."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q for q in off if q.key in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y")]
off = [q.moved(d=7.5, w=8.0) if q.key == "Y" else q for q in off]
gp = Play(off + [O("QB", "QB", -6.0, 0.0, "A")],
          [D("LB", "MIKE", 9.0, 9.2, "M"), D("E1", "DE", -4.8, -2.2, "E"), D("E2", "DE", -5.2, 2.0, "T")],
          los=14, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
fld = gp.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 27.2), window=(-14.5, 15.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
tackle_box(ax, fld, gp, -14.0)
qbB = (-7.5, 12.5)
draw_marker(ax, *XY(fld, gp, *qbB), "off", "B", fld.pts_per_yard())
path_arrow(fld, gp, [(-6.0, 0.0), (-1.0, -3.5), (6.0, -6.0)], color=RED, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [(-6.0, 0.0), (5.0, 6.0), (11.0, 9.0)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [qbB, (2.5, 24.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [qbB, (-3.2, 24.4)], color=RED, lw=1.6)
say(fld, gp, 8.6, -7.5, "1  grounding\n(safety)", color=RED, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, 12.8, 5.0, "2  legal: near Y", color=GREEN, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, 5.0, 18.4, "3  legal: out of\nbounds past the line", color=GREEN, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -11.3, 18.8, "4  grounding: short\nof the line (safety)", color=RED, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -12.4, 0.0, "tackle box\n(back to the end line)", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -3.0, -10.5, "goal line", fs=6.0)
say(fld, gp, 1.2, -16.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, gp, -9.0, -12.0, "end zone", fs=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
xs_, ys_ = XY(fld, gp, 6.0, 25.3)
ax.text(xs_, ys_, "out of bounds", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

Why draw the line at the box? The rule is balancing two things. A sack is something the defense earned:
it beat the blockers. If a quarterback could always throw the ball into the ground to avoid one, the pass
rush would lose much of its value, so inside the pocket, where the defense has him trapped, he must at least
