throw toward someone. But a quarterback who has escaped the pocket has beaten the rush himself, and he's
usually near the sideline with defenders closing; letting him throw it away (provided it reaches the line,
so he can't just dump it at his feet) rewards the escape and spares him a hit. The 2024 wording, counting
the ball or any body part outside the box, tilted that balance a little further toward the quarterback.

The most expensive grounding call of recent decades shows the safety clause at work: on New England's first
offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, February 5, 2012, Tom Brady, pressured in his own end zone, threw deep down
the middle to nobody. Grounding from the end zone is a safety, and the Giants led 2–0 before the Patriots had
gained a yard. They won by four.[^xlvi]

The "has been outside" clause is the subtle part, and it's easiest to see in motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-grounding-anim
#| fig-cap: "Once outside, always outside (simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format; an illustrative play). 0.9 s: the quarterback is in the tackle box (shaded), so a throwaway must go near a receiver. 2.1 s: pressure flushes him to his right, out of the box; the grounding exception is now on. 2.9 s: he drifts back inside the box, but he has been outside, so the exception stays on for the rest of the play. 4.3 s: he throws it away into empty space on the left, and it lands past the line of scrimmage: legal, no flag. Had it landed short of the line, it would be grounding."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.0, w=-3.5) if q.key == "WILL" else q for q in dfn]
sp = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    sp.route(k, r.go(12))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    sp.route(k, r.seam(11))
for dk, rk in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y")):
    sp.man(dk, rk)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):                  # the line sets and holds
    sp.block(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
sp.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -2.2)])                        # the back stays in to block
# the quarterback: drops, is flushed right (out of the box), then steps back up inside it
sp.path("QB", [(-2.0, 0.0), (-2.5, 7.5), (-0.8, 2.6)], speed=5.0)
sp.path("SDT", [(-0.4, 0.9)], absolute=True); sp.path("WDT", [(-0.4, -0.9)], absolute=True)
sp.path("WDE", [(-3.5, -4.5), (-7.0, -1.2), (-8.8, 0.6)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)   # flushes him, overruns
sp.path("SDE", [(-1.8, 4.6)], absolute=True)                                            # held up by the tackle...
sp.path("SDE", [(-6.0, 9.6)], absolute=True, delay=1.0)                                 # ...then closes outside
sp.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 2.5)); sp.drop("FS", (16.0, -8.0))
trk = sp.to_tracking(t_after=2.4)
trk = trk[trk.time <= 4.6].copy()
T_THROW, LAND = 3.2, (2.0, -13.0)
qb_at = sp.position("QB", T_THROW)
ball = trk.side == "ball"
pre = ball & (trk.time > 0.15) & (trk.time < T_THROW)       # carried in his right hand, not over his face
trk.loc[pre, "y"] -= 0.8
m = ball & (trk.time >= T_THROW)
tt = trk.loc[m, "time"].to_numpy()
f = np.clip((tt - T_THROW) / (np.hypot(*(np.array(LAND) - qb_at)) / 16.0), 0, 1)
bd = qb_at[0] + f * (LAND[0] - qb_at[0])
bw = qb_at[1] + f * (LAND[1] - qb_at[1])
trk.loc[m, "x"], trk.loc[m, "y"] = sp.to_abs(bd, bw)
GNOTES = [("inside the box:\nthrow near a receiver", PURPLE), ("outside:\nexception on", GREEN),
          ("back inside, but has\nbeen outside: still on", GREEN), ("lands past the line:\nlegal throwaway", GREEN)]


def g_decor(fld, t):
    tackle_box(fld.ax, fld, sp, -13.0, alpha=0.12)
    if t >= T_THROW + 0.9:
        xmark(fld, sp, *LAND, color=GREEN, ms=7)


def g_notes(fld, i, t):
    txt, col = GNOTES[i]
    say(fld, sp, -10.6, 13.5, txt, color=col, fs=6.6 if PDF else 8.0, weight="bold")


show_scene(sp, trk, [0.9, 2.1, 2.9, 4.3], window=(-13.5, 15.5), lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), decor=g_decor,
           notes=g_notes)
```

## The measurement: chains, cameras, and the spot

[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
described the chain crew and its century-old ritual: two sticks joined by ten yards of chain, carried onto
the field and stretched out to see whether the ball's nose had reached the front stick. Since 2025 that walk
is mostly gone. A [**virtual measurement**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-virtual-measurement), often
called a [**Hawk-Eye measurement**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hawk-eye-measurement) after the Sony
system that does it, uses six 8K cameras around the stadium to measure the distance from where the ball sits
to the line to gain, and hands the answer to the officials in about 30 seconds, while a virtual graphic of
the measurement plays on the broadcast and the stadium screens. The chain crew stays on the sideline as the
visible marker for players and coaches, and as a backup if the cameras fail.[^hawkeye]

```{python}
#| label: fig-measure
#| fig-cap: "What changed in 2025, and what didn't. Left, the old way: the chain crew carries the sticks onto the field, an official lays the chain's clip on the 5-yard line where it was marked, so the rear stick goes back exactly where the series began, and the front stick is compared with the nose of the ball. Right, a close-up of the same spot, about two yards across: since 2025, six cameras around the stadium measure the gap between the ball's nose and the line to gain, to a fraction of an inch. But in both, the ball sits where an official spotted it by eye (the shaded band is an illustrative margin of error, not a measured one): the cameras measure from that spot; they don't choose it."
q = Play([], None, los=62.0, ball_y="middle", to_go=None)   # d = yards past where this series began
LTG, NOSE = 10.0, 9.85                                     # line to gain; the ball's nose, about 5 inches short
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.0), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.25, 1]))


def ball_shape(ax, fld, w=0.0):
    bx, by = XY(fld, q, NOSE - 0.155, w)
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 0.19, 0.31, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))


def ltg_line(ax, fld, w0, w1):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, q, LTG, w0), XY(fld, q, LTG, w1)
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=2.2, zorder=3)


# left: the chain crew's measurement on the field
ax = axes[0]
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=69.0, window=(-8.0, 5.0), to_go=None,
            lateral=(MIDDLE - 6.5, MIDDLE + 6.5))
no_numbers(ax)
ltg_line(ax, fld, -6.5, 6.5)
ball_shape(ax, fld)
for d_ in (0.0, LTG):
    ax.plot(*XY(fld, q, d_, 0.6), marker="s", ms=6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, zorder=10)
ax.plot(*zip(XY(fld, q, 0.0, 0.6), XY(fld, q, LTG, 0.6)), color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1)), zorder=8)
ax.plot(*XY(fld, q, 3.0, 0.6), marker="D", ms=4.5, color=style.INK, zorder=10)
say(fld, q, 0.3, 3.2, "rear stick", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 3.0, 3.6, "clip laid on the\n5-yard line", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 11.0, 3.2, "front stick", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 10.9, -3.6, "line to gain", fs=6.4, color=style.INK)
say(fld, q, 8.9, -2.6, "the ball", fs=6.4, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
say(fld, q, 6.2, -3.9, "line of scrimmage", fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
ax.set_title("Until 2024: the chains walk out", fontsize=8.2, loc="left", fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# right: a close-up of the same spot, where the cameras measure
ax = axes[1]
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=62.0 + LTG, window=(-1.0, 0.75), to_go=None,
            lateral=(MIDDLE - 0.95, MIDDLE + 0.95), hashes=False, numbers=False)
ltg_line(ax, fld, -0.95, 0.95)
band = [XY(fld, q, *pt) for pt in [(NOSE - 0.33, -0.95), (NOSE - 0.33, 0.95), (NOSE + 0.33, 0.95), (NOSE + 0.33, -0.95)]]
ax.add_patch(Polygon(band, closed=True, fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.10, ec="none", zorder=2))
ball_shape(ax, fld)
(mx, my0), (_, my1) = XY(fld, q, NOSE, 0.28), XY(fld, q, LTG, 0.28)
ax.annotate("", xy=(mx, my1), xytext=(mx, my0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=GREEN, lw=1.3,
                                                                 shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=11)
say(fld, q, LTG + 0.12, 0.62, "measured:\nabout 5 inches\nshort", fs=6.4, color=GREEN, weight="bold")
say(fld, q, LTG + 0.36, -0.45, "line to gain", fs=6.4, color=style.INK)
say(fld, q, NOSE - 0.62, 0.0, "the spot, chosen by eye\n(shaded: illustrative error)", fs=6.0,
    color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Since 2025: cameras measure the gap", fontsize=8.2, loc="left", fontweight="bold",
             color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The change is a nice lesson in the difference between *precision* and *accuracy*. The chains were neither
precise (a clip laid by hand, a chain pulled taut by eye) nor fast. The cameras are extremely precise. But
they measure from the spot, and the spot is still a human judgment: an official running alongside the
play, often looking through a pile of bodies, deciding where the ball's nose was when forward progress
stopped. A measurement accurate to a fraction of an inch, taken from a spot that could be off by a foot,
is only as good as the spot. That is why the spot itself can still be reviewed, but only in narrow cases: on
a play that's challenged or booth-reviewed, the replay official can move the spot when the video clearly shows
where the ball was relative to the line to gain or the goal line.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The cameras decide first downs now." They decide the *measurement*. The officials still spot the ball by
eye, and the yellow line on your screen is still the broadcaster's drawing, not an official mark. When a
spot looks wrong, the cameras can't help; only a review of the spot can.
:::

## Reading the referee's announcement

Every announcement follows the same grammar, and once you know it you can usually finish the referee's
sentence for him. For a foul, the order is: **what** the foul was, **who** committed it (offense or defense,
and the player's number), **how much** it costs and **from where**, and **what happens to the down**.
For a review it's: the **outcome** (stands, confirmed, reversed), the **reason** in a sentence, and the
**result** (the new down, distance and spot, and anything about the clock).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-announce
#| tbl-cap: "Six announcements decoded. The words in quotation marks are the typical form; referees vary the wording a little."
rows = [
    ("“Holding, number 72, offense. Ten-yard penalty. Repeat second down.”",
     "An accepted offensive holding foul: 10 yards from the previous spot, and the down is played again."),
    ("“Pass interference, defense, number 24. Spot foul. Automatic first down.”",
     "Defensive pass interference: the ball goes to the spot of the foul with a new set of downs."),
    ("“Offsetting fouls. Repeat third down.”", "A foul by each team; they cancel and the down is replayed."),
    ("“Illegal formation, offense. The penalty is declined. Fourth down.”",
     "The defense chose the play's result over the yards (a third-down incompletion, say)."),
    ("“After review, the ruling on the field stands. Third down.”",
     "The video wasn't clear enough to overturn the call, whichever way it was."),
    ("“After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The runner's knee was down before the ball came out. "
     "There is no fumble. Second down.”",
     "The booth turned a turnover back into a tackle: the down-by-contact order of events."),
]
md_table(rows, ["What the referee says", "What it means"], [":--", ":--"])
```

The enforcement words in those sentences, *spot foul*, *declined*, *automatic first down* and the rest, are
taught in [Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd), which also explains when a
team should decline a penalty. Before the announcement, the referee's arm signal tells you most of it, and a
few signals cover most flags: a hand gripping the other wrist for holding; both hands on the hips for
offside or encroachment; forearms rolling over each other in front of the chest for a false start; both
open hands pushed forward from the shoulders for pass interference; one wrist chopping the other above the
head for a personal foul; and both open palms swung across the body to one side for intentional
grounding.[^signals]

### Do crews call games differently?

Each referee leads the same crew for a season, and fans and bettors love the idea that some crews are
"flag-happy". The data gives a measured answer.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crews
#| fig-cap: "Accepted penalties per game (both teams combined, every play) in games led by each referee's crew, 2024 (hollow) and 2025 (filled), for the referees who led a crew in both seasons, sorted by 2025. The grey band is the range around the 2025 league average that a crew would land in from game-to-game randomness alone, about two standard errors for a 16-game sample. Most crews sit inside it, and the order reshuffles from one season to the next. Source: nflverse play-by-play and officials data (regular seasons)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
ys = np.arange(len(wide))
ax.axvspan(avg25 - 2 * se_crew, avg25 + 2 * se_crew, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.7, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvline(avg25, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
for y, (name, row) in zip(ys, wide.iterrows()):
    ax.plot([row[2024], row[2025]], [y, y], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(row[2024], y, "o", ms=6, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.4, zorder=3)
    ax.plot(row[2025], y, "o", ms=6, color=style.OFFENSE, zorder=4)
ax.set_yticks(ys, wide.index, fontsize=7.2)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Accepted penalties per game", fontsize=7.6)
ax.text(avg25, len(wide) - 0.2, f"2025 average {avg25:.1f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8,
        color=style.INK_2)
h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.4, ms=6, label="2024"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.OFFENSE, ms=6, label="2025")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="lower right", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(wide) + 0.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In 2025 an average game had `{python} S["pen25"]` accepted penalties, and the crews' averages ran from
`{python} S["crew_lo"]` (`{python} S["crew_lo_name"]`'s crew) to `{python} S["crew_hi"]`
(`{python} S["crew_hi_name"]`'s).[^crewcalc] That spread sounds large until you set it against the noise. A
single game's total varies a lot (the standard deviation was about `{python} S["sd_game"]` penalties), so a
crew's 16- or 17-game average would wander about ±`{python} S["se2"]` around the league average by luck
alone. Most crews sit inside that band. And the ranking doesn't hold: the correlation between a crew's 2024
and 2025 averages was `{python} S["r2425"]`, and across the ten seasons from 2016 to 2025 the year-to-year
correlation ranged from `{python} S["r_lo"]` to `{python} S["r_hi"]`, with a median of
`{python} S["r_med"]`. Only `{python} S["same_half"]` of the `{python} S["ncrew"]` crews landed in the same
half of the table both years.

So crews differ a little, and inconsistently. Most of what makes a game flag-heavy is the game: the teams
(some offenses false-start more, some defenses hold more), the noise, the weather, the number of plays. And
some of the variation is the league's doing, not the crews': the league-wide average swings with points of
emphasis, from `{python} S["pen_lo"]` to `{python} S["pen_hi"]` per game across 2016–2025, which is why a
preseason memo telling officials to watch for a particular foul can move the numbers for every crew at once.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cowboys at Packers, 2014 divisional playoffs, the catch that wasn't"}
Find the play: January 11, 2015, fourth quarter, 4:42 left, fourth-and-2 at the Green Bay 32, Dallas down
26–21. Watch Dez Bryant from the moment the ball arrives, and count the gates. Control: yes, he has it in
his hands above the cornerback. Feet: yes, he lands and takes steps. Time: here is the argument. He takes
three steps while falling and stretches the ball toward the goal line, and the ball hits the turf and moves
as he lands. Under the 2014 rule, he was going to the ground in the process of the catch, so he had to
keep control through the ground, and replay ruled he hadn't. Under the 2018 rule, the reach is an act common
to the game, which finishes the catch before the ball touches down. Watch the replay twice, once with each
rule in your head, and you'll understand why the league changed it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots at Steelers, 2017, survive the ground"}
December 17, 2017, 34 seconds left, Steelers down 27–24, first-and-10 at the New England 10. Jesse James
catches a short pass, goes to a knee at about the 1, and lunges across the goal line; the ball moves as it
hits the turf. Notice first who reviewed it: under two minutes, and a scoring play, so it was the booth,
not a challenge. Then notice the clause that decided it, the same going-to-the-ground language as the
Bryant play. Two plays later Ben Roethlisberger faked a spike and threw an interception in the end zone.
Three months later the rule was gone.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots at Jets, 2017, the touchback nobody recovered"}
October 15, 2017, fourth quarter, 8:31 left, the Jets down 24–14 at the New England 4. Austin
Seferian-Jenkins catches a short pass and turns toward the goal line; as he dives, the ball comes loose in
the defender's hands. Ruled a touchdown, it went to the booth as a scoring play. Replay ruled he lost the
ball before crossing the line, and that it then went out of bounds in the end zone. Watch the referee's
announcement: no defender recovered anything, and the Patriots got the ball at their own 20. New England
won by seven. Then watch the ball-carrying hand: the ball was in his outside arm, but on the dive he
extended it toward the pylon, where the defender's hand could reach it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chargers at Broncos, 2008, the whistle"}
September 14, 2008, 1:17 left, Denver down 38–31, second-and-goal at the San Diego 1. Watch Jay Cutler's
arm. It never comes forward with the ball; the ball slips out as he winds up. Then listen for the whistle,
and watch the Chargers stop and start, unsure whether the play is alive. The rules of the time gave replay
no way to award the recovery after the whistle. Today's officials would let the scramble finish, rule a
fumble, and let replay confirm it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: the 2025 season, the cameras arrive"}
Pick any 2025 or 2026 game and wait for a close spot on third or fourth down. Watch the order of events: the
official spots the ball by eye, the referee signals for a measurement, and within about half a minute the
stadium screen shows the virtual line against the ball's nose. The chain crew never leaves the sideline. Then
watch the reactions: players and coaches now argue about the spot, the only human part left, and almost
never about the measurement.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the ref's mic"}
Every time a flag flies, or a ruling is close, make two calls before the referee turns on his microphone:

1. **Name the official.** Who threw it? A flag from the line of scrimmage at a sideline is the down or line
   judge (pre-snap foul, likely false start, offside or illegal formation). A flag from deep downfield is a
   side, field or back judge (likely pass interference or illegal contact). A flag from the backfield, near
   the quarterback, is the referee (roughing the passer, grounding) or the umpire (holding in the middle).
2. **Name the foul or the ruling**, and its result: how many yards, from where, and the down that follows.
3. **On every review, predict the outcome**: *reversed*, *confirmed* or *stands*. First ask who started it
   (a coach's flag, or the booth: under two minutes, a score, a turnover). Then ask which angle would settle
   it. If the decisive moment is hidden (a pile, a body in the way), say *stands*.
4. **On every close catch, count the gates out loud**: control, feet, time.

Keep a tally for one game: officials named correctly, fouls named correctly, review outcomes called
correctly. Most viewers get the foul right about half the time at first; by the end of a season the
official-then-foul habit will have you announcing it before the referee does. Add your review predictions to
your prediction log.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the sideline catch"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sideline
#| fig-cap: "Second quarter, 1:52 left. The receiver (Z) catches a pass running toward the right sideline at the opponent's 38, gets his right foot down in bounds, then his left, and is knocked out of bounds by the cornerback; the ball comes loose as he hits the ground beyond the sideline. The field judge (FJ) rules it incomplete. The offense's head coach reaches for his red flag."
off = [O("QB", "QB", -6.5, -1.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 14.5, "C"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.0, "S")]
pp = Play(off, dfn, los=58, ball_y="right", to_go=6)
pp.route("Z", [(0, 0), (9.0, 0.5), (14.0, 10.0)], side=+1)
pp.path("RCB", [(11.5, 17.5), (13.4, 21.6)], absolute=True)
pp.pass_to("Z", t=1.6)
fld = pp.draw(lateral=(-8.5, 32.0), window=(-9.0, 25.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
official(ax, *XY(fld, pp, 19.0, 27.0), "FJ", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=1.3)
for (dd, ww), lab in [((13.4, 22.4), "1"), ((14.4, 23.3), "2")]:
    x_, y_ = XY(fld, pp, dd, ww)
    ax.plot(x_, y_, marker="o", ms=5.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=11, mec="white", mew=0.6)
    say(fld, pp, dd + (0.0 if lab == "1" else 0.9), ww - 1.2 if lab == "1" else ww - 0.2, lab, fs=6.4,
        color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold", box=False)
ball_at(fld, pp, 15.6, 25.4)
say(fld, pp, 17.6, 15.6, "two feet down\nin bounds", fs=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pp, 11.8, 28.2, "ball comes\nloose as he\nlands out", fs=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pp, 3.0, 24.6, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
plt.show()
```

**Can the coach challenge? Who decides, and what will the review look for?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**He can't challenge**: it's inside the final two minutes of the half, so only the booth can review it,
and the coach's flag would be wasted (a coach who throws one when he isn't allowed to is charged a timeout,
or yards if he has none left). The replay official decides whether to stop the game; if he does, New York
rules, and the referee announces it.
<!-- VERIFY: the current consequence of a challenge flag thrown inside two minutes (timeout charged vs 15-yard unsportsmanlike penalty). -->

The review runs the three gates. **Control**: did he have the ball secured before it touched anything?
**Feet**: did both feet come down in bounds, the right and then the left, while he had control? If yes, the
first two gates are passed. **Time**: a toe-tap along the sideline leaves no time for an act common to
the game before he goes out, so he had to **keep control through his landing out of bounds**. The ball came
loose when he hit the ground, so if the video shows it, the answer is **"the ruling on the field stands"**
or **"is confirmed": incomplete**. If the video instead shows him landing with the ball still secured and
it coming loose only as he rolled over afterward, it's **reversed: a catch**, and because he was out of
bounds the ball is dead there, not a fumble.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: reaching for the pylon"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-pylon
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-goal from the 3, third quarter. The running back (R) bounces outside and dives for the pylon. At the 1, a safety's punch knocks the ball out of his outside arm; it bounces into the end zone and rolls out of bounds through the side of the end zone. Nobody touches it after the punch."
rb = O("RB", "RB", -4.5, 4.0, "R")
pz = Play([rb, O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q")] + [O(k, k, -0.7, w, "") for k, w in [("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2)]],
          [D("SS", "SS", 2.2, 9.0, "S"), D("CB", "CB", 3.4, 14.0, "C")], los=107, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
pz.run("RB", [(-1.0, 8.5), (1.5, 13.5)], absolute=True)
pz.path("SS", [(1.9, 13.0)], absolute=True)
fld = pz.draw(lateral=(-6.5, 30.0), window=(-6.5, 13.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
xmark(fld, pz, 2.0, 14.2)
path_arrow(fld, pz, [(2.0, 14.2), (4.8, 17.6), (7.5, 23.58), (8.0, 24.8)])
say(fld, pz, -2.5, 25.2, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, pz, 3.6, 4.0, "goal line", fs=6.2)
say(fld, pz, 11.8, 12.0, "end line", fs=6.2)
say(fld, pz, 1.4, 20.5, "punched\nout at the 1", fs=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pz, 8.6, 17.0, "out of bounds\nin the end zone", fs=6.6, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

**What's the ruling, and who gets the ball where? What if the ball had gone out of bounds at the 1 instead?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A fumble through the end zone: touchback.** The ball was fumbled forward into the opponent's end zone and
went out of bounds there, so the defense takes over at its own 20, even though it never recovered the ball.
Because it's a turnover, the booth reviews it automatically; the only questions are whether the ball came
out before the runner's knee or body touched the ground (if his knee was down first, he was down by contact
at the 1, and it's fourth-and-goal from there) and whether it crossed the goal line before going out.

If the ball had gone out of bounds *at the 1*, short of the goal line, the offense would keep it. And
because a fumble that goes out forward comes back to the spot of the fumble, it would be at the 1, where the
punch knocked it out: fourth-and-goal. The difference between those two outcomes is a few feet of turf and
roughly a touchdown's worth of expected points, which is why coaches tell runners to carry the ball high
and tight near the goal line instead of reaching for the pylon.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the dropped screen"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-screen
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10. The quarterback, in the shotgun, catches the snap five yards deep and immediately throws to the slot receiver (H), who has bowed back to receive a bubble screen. The receiver is a yard behind the spot where the quarterback released the ball when the pass bounces off his hands and onto the turf. The nickel defender ($) scoops it up and runs the other way while most players stop."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q.moved(d=-6.2, w=-7.0) if q.key == "H" else q for q in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", offense("gun_2x2"))
dfn = [q.moved(d=3.5, w=-8.5) if q.key == "NB" else q for q in dfn]
ps = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=10)
ps.path("NB", [(-6.8, -8.2), (-11.0, -6.0)], absolute=True)
fld = ps.draw(lateral=(-20.0, 20.0), window=(-13.0, 15.0), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
x0_, y0_ = XY(fld, ps, -5.3, -18.8)
x1_, y1_ = XY(fld, ps, -5.3, 18.8)
ax.plot([x0_, x1_], [y0_, y1_], color=PURPLE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)
say(fld, ps, -4.4, 15.0, "release line", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
path_arrow(fld, ps, [(-5.3, 0.2), (-6.2, -6.2)], lw=1.5)
xmark(fld, ps, -7.3, -6.0, color=style.BALL, ms=7)
say(fld, ps, -8.6, -1.6, "drops it here", fs=6.6, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
say(fld, ps, -10.6, -10.8, "scoops it up,\nruns it back", fs=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

**Do you keep watching the nickel defender? What's the ruling?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Keep watching.** The receiver was behind the yard line where the quarterback released the ball, so the
pass traveled backward: it was a **backward pass**, not a forward pass. A dropped backward pass is a live
ball, like a fumble, so the defender's recovery counts and he may advance it. If he scores, it's a
defensive touchdown (and, as a change of possession and a score, the booth reviews it, looking at exactly
one thing: whether the ball traveled forward). The officials will usually let this play run rather than
blow a whistle, for the reason in the 2008 story: replay can take a touchdown away cleanly, but can't hand
the defense a recovery it was whistled out of.

Had the receiver caught it a yard *ahead* of the release point, which is where most shotgun screens are
caught, the same drop would be an incomplete forward pass and a dead ball. Defenders are coached to scoop
up every dropped screen for exactly this reason.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Seven officials split the field and the players.** The referee (white cap) watches the quarterback and
  announces; the umpire watches the interior line; the down and line judges own the line of scrimmage and the
  sidelines; the side, field and back judges own the receivers downfield. Who threw a flag tells you what it
  is likely to be.
- **Replay has three doors.** Coaches challenge (two, a third if either succeeds since 2024, a timeout lost
  if they fail, never inside two minutes of a half). The booth reviews scores, turnovers, tries and the final
  two minutes. Replay assist fixes objective facts and, since 2025, wipes out certain flags; since 2026 the
  league may consult on ejections. Judgment fouls aren't reviewable, and there is no sky judge. Changes
  require clear and obvious evidence, so a hidden moment usually "stands".
- **A catch is three gates: control, feet down, then time** (an act common to the game, or long enough to
  make one). The 2018 rewrite removed the survive-the-ground clause after the Johnson, Bryant and James
  rulings, trading an objective test for one that matches what people see.
- **The order of events decides possession.** Ball out before the knee is a fumble; knee down after
  contact first is a tackle; untouched, an NFL runner isn't down. Forward progress sets the spot. Officials
  hold the whistle on close fumbles because replay can undo a fumble but can't invent a recovery.
- **The rules of the ball are about direction and territory.** A forward fumble out of bounds comes back to
  the spot of the fumble, but into the opponent's end zone and out it's a touchback. A pass that doesn't go
  forward, parallel included, is a backward pass and stays live if dropped. Grounding is a foul only inside
  the tackle box, or short of the line; once a passer has been outside the box, a throwaway just has to
  reach the line.
- **Cameras measure, people spot.** Hawk-Eye has replaced the chain walk since 2025, but it measures from a
  spot an official chose by eye. Crew differences in flags are real but small and unstable from year to year.

**Builds on:** [Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd) (the fouls these
officials call, and how they are enforced: spot fouls, accept or decline, half the distance) and
[Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) (the throwaway, and why a quarterback
leaves the pocket). The spot, forward progress and the chain crew were introduced in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd); the
end zone and the plane of the goal line in
[The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd); the touchback on
kicks in [Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game](09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd); the challenge
decision and the staff who advise on it in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd); and why tempo offenses hurry
to beat a challenge in
[In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd).

**Sets up:** [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd),
where spikes, grounding, the booth's control of the final two minutes and the value of a timeout spent on a
challenge all become clock decisions; and
[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd),
where forward progress and the goal-line spot decide the tush push and every fourth-and-inches. The rules'
history (the 1978 passing changes, the catch rule, replay) is placed in context in
[The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) and Appendix E, and Part 13 shows how to
pull the review and penalty data behind this chapter's charts yourself
([nflverse in Python](../13-analytics-and-data/13-01-nflverse-in-python.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- The **NFL Rulebook** (NFL Football Operations, free online): Rule 3 (definitions, including the catch and
  the pocket area), Rule 7 (dead ball, down by contact), Rule 8 (forward and backward passes, intentional
  grounding, fumbles), Rule 11 (touchbacks) and Rule 15 (instant replay). The league also publishes
  officiating videos explaining recent rulings, with the same angles the replay officials use.
- **Football Zebras** (footballzebras.com), written by former officials and longtime followers of
  officiating: crew assignments, rule changes and play-by-play explanations of controversial calls.
- **nflverse** (via `nflreadpy`): `load_officials()` for every game's crew since 2015 and the play-by-play
  `desc` text for every recorded review and penalty, enough to rebuild both charts in this chapter and test
  your own theories about crews.
- Former NFL officiating chiefs (Mike Pereira, Dean Blandino) explain controversial calls on broadcasts and
  in columns every week; following them is the fastest way to learn how the people in the booth think.
:::
